stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD HITS DECADE HIGH 4.68% — RUSSELL 2000 DROPS OVER 1% AS RATES SQUEEZE EQUITIES
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield climbed another 5 basis points to 4.68% Tuesday — its highest level in over a decade — as fiscal concerns and inflation expectations continue to build beyond last week's Moody's-linked selloff. The S&P 500 fell 0.42% to 7,372 and the Russell 2000 tumbled over 1%, with rising risk-free rates compressing the equity risk premium most severely in small-caps and long-duration growth names.

stories.headline: AI STOCKS FALL FOR SECOND DAY AHEAD OF NVIDIA EARNINGS TOMORROW
stories.body: Nvidia, Seagate, Meta, and Tesla all finished firmly lower Tuesday as AI infrastructure stocks pulled back ahead of Nvidia's Q1 earnings report Wednesday. Seagate futures were down approximately 10% on the week. With the 10-year at 4.68%, the market is stress-testing whether AI earnings growth can justify current multiples under materially higher discount rates — Nvidia's guidance tomorrow is the defining data point.

stories.headline: TRUMP CALLS OFF IRAN MILITARY STRIKE, CITES 'SERIOUS NEGOTIATIONS' — OIL DROPS TO $104
stories.body: President Trump said he canceled a planned strike on Iran that had been expected Tuesday, citing active peace talks facilitated by Gulf states toward a deal acceptable to the U.S. WTI crude fell 1.9% to $104/bbl — a $2 drop from Monday's close of $106 — as the immediate strike risk premium deflated, though the broader Middle East risk floor remains with negotiations still unresolved.

stories.headline: WHO DECLARES EBOLA A GLOBAL HEALTH EMERGENCY AS OUTBREAK HITS CONGO AND UGANDA
stories.body: The World Health Organization declared the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda Ebola outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on Sunday, adding a fresh risk-off layer to an already volatile week. Markets have not priced material impact yet, but the declaration raises concern about Central African mining supply chains and adds to a crowded macro risk calendar.

stories.headline: NCAA EXPANDS MARCH MADNESS TO 76 TEAMS FOR 2026-27; PORTAL ACTIVE AS ROSTERS FINALIZE
stories.body: The NCAA confirmed it will expand both the men's and women's basketball tournaments to 76 teams starting next season, adding three automatic bids. The May 27 NBA Draft withdrawal deadline is the next major roster-shaping event — players who return will trigger the remaining transfer dominoes, with Florida, Louisville, and Indiana currently leading the rebuilt portal standings.

stories.headline: WEMBANYAMA DELIVERS 41/24 IN DOUBLE OT AS SPURS STUN THUNDER IN WCF GAME 1
stories.body: Victor Wembanyama scored 41 points and grabbed 24 rebounds Monday night as San Antonio beat Oklahoma City 122-115 in double overtime — one of the most complete playoff performances in recent memory — to take a 1-0 lead in the Western Conference Finals. Tonight in the East, the Cavaliers (who eliminated Detroit 125-94 in Game 7 Sunday) open the ECF against New York at MSG, tip 8:30 PM ET.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS OPEN SUPER BOWL DEFENSE VS. PATRIOTS SEPT 9; WEEK 2 OF OTAS UNDERWAY
stories.body: The defending Super Bowl LX champion Seahawks (who beat New England 29-13 in February) will open their title defense against the Patriots on September 9, with a franchise-record six primetime games on their 2026 schedule. Around the league, OTA week two sessions continue Tuesday with Rodgers taking first-team reps in Pittsburgh for a second straight day.

stories.headline: MENSAH SETTLES WITH DUKE, COMMITS TO MIAMI; LSU TOPS PORTAL CYCLE WITH LEAVITT AND LONGSTREET
stories.body: Quarterback Darian Mensah resolved his legal dispute with Duke and committed to Miami as the Hurricanes' 2026 starter, the most notable resolution of the May portal window. Nationally, LSU emerged as the portal cycle's biggest winner — landing No. 1-ranked QB Sam Leavitt and former USC five-star Husan Longstreet alongside multiple four-star additions at skill and defensive line.

deepDive.title: The Term Premium: Why Treasury Yields Surge Without Fed Rate Hikes
content: The 10-year Treasury yield hit 4.68% today — a decade high — even though the Federal Reserve has held the federal funds rate steady and hasn't signaled an imminent hike. That disconnect exposes something most people miss: long-term yields aren't just a projection of where the Fed sets short rates. They embed a separate component called the 'term premium' — the extra return investors demand for committing capital for ten years instead of rolling over short-term bills. When that premium rises, yields go up independent of monetary policy, and that is exactly what is happening now.

The term premium has two layers. First: uncertainty. The longer the bond, the more rate paths a market must price across — any estimate of where short rates will be in Year 8 is a guess, and investors charge for that uncertainty. Second: credit and fiscal risk. If bondholders begin to doubt the U.S. will honor obligations without inflating them away, they demand higher yields as compensation. After Moody's stripped the U.S. of its last triple-A rating in May 2025 — citing deficits projected at 7% of GDP annually through 2035 and federal debt on track for 134% of GDP — investors began embedding a growing fiscal risk premium into long-duration bonds. That premium is compounding now: the ACM model at the New York Fed estimates term premiums are roughly 100 basis points above their post-financial-crisis lows, where they sat near zero from 2012 through 2021.

The last time term premiums surged without Fed action was 1994, when Alan Greenspan raised rates 300 basis points in 12 months and bond markets globally collapsed in what traders called the 'bond market massacre.' Today's dynamic is structurally different but equally powerful: the Fed is doing quantitative tightening (removing itself as a buyer), Japan and China have been reducing Treasury holdings, and the U.S. Treasury is issuing record supply to fund the deficit — all colliding at the long end of the curve. The net result is that no single large buyer can absorb the supply, so yields must rise to attract marginal demand. This is a mechanics problem, not a policy problem — and it doesn't resolve with a pivot in the fed funds rate.

For today's market setup, the implications are direct. As the 10-year approaches 4.7% and the 30-year edges above 5.1%, pension funds and insurers running liability-driven investing strategies face mathematical pressure to reduce equity exposure — their asset-liability models require them to buy bonds as yields rise, selling stocks in the process. This is structural, non-discretionary selling from the largest pool of capital in the world. It also squeezes the equity risk premium: at a 4.68% risk-free rate, expected stock returns must be meaningfully higher to justify the risk. That's the exact pressure hitting Nasdaq today — and why Nvidia's guidance tomorrow matters so much. If AI earnings can grow fast enough to outpace rising discount rates, the growth trade survives. If they can't, the yield-driven derating of long-duration assets accelerates.
